latest_nl_proof:
Fix an integer m>=2 and a tuple k=(k_1,…,k_{m-1}) of positive integers satisfying the stated Kunz inequalities.

Define
S(k)=\{qm+r\in \mathbb N_0: q,r\in \mathbb Z,\ q\ge 0,\ 0\le r\le m-1,\text{ and }(r=0\text{ or }q\ge k_r)\}.

We prove all claimed properties.

First, 0\in S(k). Indeed, take q=0 and r=0; then 0=0\cdot m+0, with q\ge 0 and 0\le r\le m-1, and since r=0 the extra inequality is automatic. So 0\in S(k).

Next we prove closure under addition. Let a,b\in S(k). Choose representations

a=q_1m+r_1, \qquad b=q_2m+r_2,

with q_1,q_2\ge 0, 0\le r_1,r_2\le m-1, and with the defining condition that if r_t\ne 0 then q_t\ge k_{r_t} for t=1,2.

We must show a+b\in S(k). We consider cases according to r_1,r_2.

Case 1: r_1=0 and r_2=0.
Then a+b=(q_1+q_2)m has residue 0 mod m, with quotient q_1+q_2\ge 0. Hence a+b\in S(k).

Case 2: exactly one of r_1,r_2 is 0.
Without loss of generality r_1=0 and r_2=s with 1\le s\le m-1. Then

a+b=(q_1+q_2)m+s.
Since b\in S(k) and s\ne 0, we have q_2\ge k_s. Therefore q_1+q_2\ge q_2\ge k_s, so the element (q_1+q_2)m+s lies in S(k). Thus a+b\in S(k).

Case 3: r_1,r_2\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}.
Then q_1\ge k_{r_1} and q_2\ge k_{r_2}. Put s=r_1+r_2.

If s<m, then

a+b=(q_1+q_2)m+s.
We need q_1+q_2\ge k_s. Since the Kunz inequalities are stated for indices i,j with 1\le i\le j\le m-1, reorder r_1,r_2 if necessary: let i=\min(r_1,r_2), j=\max(r_1,r_2). Then 1\le i\le j\le m-1 and i+j=s<m, so the hypothesis gives
k_i+k_j\ge k_s.
Because q_1\ge k_{r_1} and q_2\ge k_{r_2}, we get
q_1+q_2\ge k_{r_1}+k_{r_2}=k_i+k_j\ge k_s.
Hence a+b\in S(k).

If s=m, then

a+b=(q_1+q_2+1)m,
which has residue 0 mod m and quotient q_1+q_2+1\ge 0. So a+b\in S(k).

If s>m, then write t=s-m, so 1\le t\le m-1, and

a+b=(q_1+q_2+1)m+t.
Again let i=\min(r_1,r_2), j=\max(r_1,r_2). Then 1\le i\le j\le m-1 and i+j=s>m, so the Kunz hypothesis gives
k_i+k_j+1\ge k_{i+j-m}=k_t.
Thus
q_1+q_2+1\ge k_{r_1}+k_{r_2}+1=k_i+k_j+1\ge k_t.
Therefore (q_1+q_2+1)m+t\in S(k), so a+b\in S(k).

All cases are covered, so S(k) is closed under addition.

Now we prove that \mathbb N_0\setminus S(k) is finite. For residue 0 modulo m, every number qm with q\ge 0 lies in S(k) by definition. For each fixed residue r with 1\le r\le m-1, the numbers congruent to r mod m that lie in S(k) are exactly those of the form qm+r with q\ge k_r. Therefore the numbers of residue r that are not in S(k) are among
\{r,\ m+r,\ 2m+r,\dots,(k_r-1)m+r\},
which is a finite set (possibly empty if k_r=0, though here each k_r\ge 1). Hence
\mathbb N_0\setminus S(k)\subseteq \bigcup_{r=1}^{m-1}\{qm+r:0\le q<k_r\},
which is a finite union of finite sets. So \mathbb N_0\setminus S(k) is finite.

Thus S(k) is a numerical semigroup in the sense stated: it contains 0, is closed under addition, and has finite complement in \mathbb N_0.

We now show that its least positive element is m.

First, m\in S(k): take q=1 and r=0, so m=1\cdot m+0.

Now let x\in S(k) with x>0. Write x=qm+r in the defining form, where q\ge 0 and 0\le r\le m-1.

If r=0, then x=qm and x>0 imply q\ge 1, hence x\ge m.

If r\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}, then by definition q\ge k_r, and since each k_r is positive we have q\ge 1. Therefore
x=qm+r\ge m+1>m.

So every positive element of S(k) is at least m, and m itself belongs to S(k). Hence m is the least positive element of S(k).

Finally, fix r with 1\le r\le m-1. We prove that the least element of S(k) congruent to r modulo m is exactly r+mk_r.

First, r+mk_r\in S(k): take q=k_r and residue r. Since k_r>0, certainly q\ge 0, and because q=k_r\ge k_r, the defining condition holds. Hence r+mk_r\in S(k).

Now let x\in S(k) satisfy x\equiv r\pmod m. Because 0\le r\le m-1 and the residue representative in the definition is unique in this range, x must be of the form x=qm+r for some integer q\ge 0. Since r\ne 0 and x\in S(k), the defining condition forces q\ge k_r. Therefore
x=qm+r\ge mk_r+r.
Thus every element of S(k) congruent to r mod m is at least r+mk_r, and that value itself lies in S(k). So
\min\{x\in S(k): x\equiv r\pmod m\}=r+mk_r.

This proves every part of the lemma.
role_in_parent: Provides the inverse construction from admissible Kunz vectors to numerical semigroups.
statement_nl: Let m be an integer with m >= 2. Let k = (k_1, ..., k_{m-1}) be a tuple of positive integers satisfying the Kunz inequalities: for all integers i and j with 1 <= i <= j <= m-1, if i + j < m then k_i + k_j >= k_{i+j}, and if i + j > m then k_i + k_j + 1 >= k_{i+j-m}. Define a subset S(k) of N0 = {0,1,2,...} by S(k) = {q m + r : q and r are integers, q >= 0, 0 <= r <= m-1, and either r = 0 or q >= k_r}. Then S(k) is a numerical semigroup, meaning that 0 belongs to S(k), S(k) is closed under addition, and N0 \ S(k) is finite. Its least positive element is m. For each integer r with 1 <= r <= m-1, the least element of S(k) congruent to r modulo m is exactly r + m k_r.

domain_restrictions: m is an integer with m >= 2
For each index t with 1 <= t <= m-1, k_t is a positive integer (k_t >= 1)
In Kunz inequalities: i and j are integers with 1 <= i <= j <= m-1
Kunz inequalities split by comparison of i+j with m: case (i+j < m) uses index i+j in [1,m-1]; case (i+j > m) uses index i+j-m in [1,m-1]
Definition of S(k): elements x are in N0; membership requires existence of integers q,res with q >= 0 and 0 <= res <= m-1
In definition of S(k): if res = 0 then the condition on q is dropped; if res ∈ {1,...,m-1} then require q >= k_res
In the final statement: residue index r satisfies 1 <= r <= m-1 (so r != 0)
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: Let m ∈ Z with m >= 2 and let k = (k_1,...,k_{m-1}) with each k_t ∈ Z_{>0}. Assume (Kunz inequalities) that for all i,j ∈ Z with 1 <= i <= j <= m-1: if i+j < m then k_i + k_j >= k_{i+j}, and if i+j > m then k_i + k_j + 1 >= k_{i+j-m}. Define S(k) ⊆ N0 by x ∈ S(k) iff ∃ q,res ∈ Z such that q >= 0, 0 <= res <= m-1, x = q*m + res, and (res=0 or q >= k_res). Then: (a) 0 ∈ S(k), (b) ∀ a,b ∈ S(k), a+b ∈ S(k), (c) N0\S(k) is finite, (d) m is the least positive element of S(k), and (e) for every r ∈ {1,...,m-1}, the minimum of {x ∈ S(k) : x ≡ r (mod m)} exists and equals r + m*k_r.
quantifier_order: ∃ k ∈ (Z_{>0})^{m-1} such that  ∀ i,j ∈ Z ( (1 <= i <= j <= m-1) ∧ (i+j < m) -> k_i + k_j >= k_{i+j} ) ∧ ( (1 <= i <= j <= m-1) ∧ (i+j > m) -> k_i + k_j + 1 >= k_{i+j-m} )  [Kunz inequalities]
Define S(k) = { x ∈ N0 : ∃ q,res ∈ Z ( q >= 0 ∧ 0 <= res <= m-1 ∧ x = q*m + res ∧ (res = 0 ∨ q >= k_res) ) }
Then: (i) 0 ∈ S(k)  ∧ (ii) ∀ a,b ∈ S(k), a+b ∈ S(k)  ∧ (iii) N0 \ S(k) is finite
Least positive element: m ∈ S(k) ∧ ∀ x ∈ S(k) (x > 0 -> m <= x)
∀ r ∈ Z (1 <= r <= m-1 ->  min{ x ∈ S(k) : x ≡ r (mod m) } = r + m*k_r )

variables.name: m
variables.role: multiplicity parameter; also defines tuple length and modular classes

variables.name: k_i
variables.role: component of k for i in [1,m-1], required to be positive; used in Kunz inequalities and membership thresholds

variables.name: i
variables.role: index for Kunz inequalities, with constraint 1 <= i <= j <= m-1

variables.name: j
variables.role: index for Kunz inequalities, with constraint 1 <= i <= j <= m-1

variables.name: q
variables.role: quotient in representation of elements of S(k): element = q*m + residue

variables.name: res
variables.role: residue class representative in [0,m-1] used in definition of S(k)

variables.name: x
variables.role: generic element for statements of membership/order/minimality within S(k)

variables.name: r
variables.role: residue class index in the final minimality statement (1 <= r <= m-1)

witness_dependencies: Membership witness for x ∈ S(k): existential witnesses (q,res) satisfy x = q*m + res and the inequality guard (res = 0 ∨ q >= k_res); thus q depends on x and res, and res is constrained to [0,m-1]
The specific claimed minimal element for a fixed residue r depends deterministically on k: candidate = r + m*k_r
For least-element property: the lower bound part quantifies over all x ∈ S(k) with x ≡ r (mod m); the minimizing x is witnessed by the explicit candidate r + m*k_r
